newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British factory gate prices fall in June.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British factory gate prices fall in June.

text.p: Prices of British goods leaving factory gates fell by 0.2 percent in June, their largest drop since July 1996, the Office for National Statistics said on Monday.
Analysts said the figures showed inflationary pressures in Britain's sluggish manufacturing sector remained weak and boded well for the country's crucial retail price inflation rate.
The decline in June output prices reverses May's 0.2 percent rise but takes the yearly growth rate up to 1.1 percent from 1.0 percent in May.

The strength of the pound provided some good news for hard pressed manufacturers, further trimming prices of fuel and raw materials and leaving scope for relatively healthy profit margins. Input prices fell 0.8 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis, after a moderate increase of 0.6 percent in May.

On a year-on-year basis, input prices registered their 13th successive monthly drop, at 8.6 percent, forced lower by weaker prices for oil and other commodities, reflecting sterling's meteoric gain of some 25 percent since last August.

"Lower input prices will help mitigate the trouble the exchange rate is causing for manufacturers. Their margins are probably still growing because of these low costs," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
The high level of sterling has made British exports more expensive in foreign currency terms, leading some manufacturers to cut prices in order to remain competitive.
The ONS said that printing and publishing prices had fallen by 1.7 percent between May and June as companies struggled to maintain their competitive edge.
Analysts warn there was little chance of an early halt to the pound's progress while expectations remain of further rises in official interest rates.

The Bank of England, with its eyes on the inflation horizon two year's ahead, raised interest rates to 6.75 percent, from 6.5 last week, the third rise in as many months. Some economists say rates could rise again as early as next month.

The producer price figures underlined the lack of upward pressure from the manufacturing side on Britain's targeted inflation measure -- retail price inflation (RPI.) Underlying RPI grew an annual 2.7 percent in June, up from the target level of 2.5.

"Inflation in the manufacturing sector is practically non-existent and with sterling continuing to strengthen there is every prospect that this well remain the case for some time," said UBS economist Andrew Cates.
"As such the prospects for retail price inflation remain excellent."
The fall in factory gate prices allows retailers to allow their customers to benefit from the lower costs that they themselves are paying and this should help to keep down prices at a retail level.
Economists said retailers will need to pass on the fall in wholesale prices if they want to maintain the current high levels of demand amongst Britain's price-sensitive consumers.

But there was some suggestion that the recent falls in output prices might be drawing to an end with the annualised growth rate of core output prices, which exclude erratic compoenets food, drink, tobacco and petrol creeping up to 1.1 percent in June from 0.8 in May. The measure is now at its highest level since May 1996.
